scenes.title:
[[Multi-Agent]] Systems
in Java
scenes.subtitle: What they are, why they help, and when NOT to use them

lines.say: One agent can do a lot. But give it too many jobs, and it starts to struggle.
In this series, you'll learn multi-agent systems in plain Java, step by step.
Today: what a multi-agent system is, when it's worth it, and your first two-agent team.

scenes.heading: What is a [[multi-agent]] system?
items: Each has its **own system prompt**: its role and rules
Each has its **own tools** and its **own context**
They **work together**: one agent's output is another's input

card.title: THE IDEA
card.code:
agent  = LLM + tools + loop
team   = agent + agent + ...

lines.say: So, what is a multi-agent system?
Remember: an agent is an LLM, plus tools, plus a loop. A multi-agent system is several of them, each with one job.
Each agent gets its own system prompt. That's its role, and its rules.
Its own tools, and its own context: the conversation it sees.
And they work together. One agent's output becomes another agent's input.
Think of a team of specialists, instead of one person doing everything.

scenes.heading: Why [[split]] the work?

rows.label: Focus
rows.text: One job, one short prompt, done well

rows.label: Clean context
rows.text: Each agent sees only what it needs

rows.label: Parallel work
rows.text: Independent agents can run at the same time

scenes.banner: Each agent has its own context window

lines.say: Why split the work? Three reasons.
One: focus. An agent with one job and a short prompt does that job better.
Two: clean context. Each agent sees only what it needs, not every file and every message.
Three: parallel work. Agents that don't depend on each other can run at the same time.
The key idea: each agent has its own context window. That's its working memory.

scenes.heading: The [[cost]] of more agents

rows.label: More tokens
rows.text: Anthropic measured ~15× a chat for multi-agent

rows.label: Harder to debug
rows.text: More moving parts, more places to fail

rows.label: More to build
rows.text: More code, more prompts to tune

scenes.banner: Start with one agent. Split only when it struggles.

lines.say: Now the honest part. More agents have a real cost.
More tokens. Anthropic wrote that their multi-agent research system used about fifteen times more tokens than a chat.
lines.tts: More tokens. Anthropic wrote that their multi-agent research system used about fifteen times more tokens than a chat.

lines.say: Harder to debug. More moving parts means more places to fail.
And more to build: more code, and more prompts to tune.
So the rule is simple. Start with one agent. Split only when it struggles.

left.title: Split when…
left.body:
• The task has clear,
  separate parts
• Too much information
  for one context
• Many different tools
  confuse one agent

right.title: Keep one agent when…
right.body:
• One agent already
  does the job well
• Every step needs
  the same context
• The parts depend
  heavily on each other

lines.say: So when should you split?
When the task has clear, separate parts. When there's too much information for one context. Or when too many tools confuse a single agent.
Keep one agent when it already works, or when every step needs the same context. Splitting those just adds cost.

left.title: One agent does it all
left.body:
Read the code
Find the bugs
Explain them kindly

One prompt, three jobs:
strict reviewer AND
friendly teacher

right.title: Two focused agents
right.body:
Reviewer: reads the file,
lists real bugs (has a tool)

Writer: turns the notes
into a friendly report
(no tools, never sees code)

✓ One job each

lines.say: Our use case is the project for this whole series: a code-review team for Java code.
One agent could read the code, find the bugs, and explain them. But that's one prompt asking for a strict reviewer and a friendly teacher at the same time.
So we split it. A Reviewer that reads the file and lists the bugs. And a Writer that turns those notes into a friendly report. It has no tools, and never sees the code.
Here's the agent from episode one.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"

    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- The official Anthropic Java SDK -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.anthropic</groupId>
            <artifactId>anthropic-java</artifactId>
            <version>3.3.0</version>

    </dependencies>

    <build>

lines.say: The model and the tools are hard-coded inside main.
And the loop lives in main too. To build a second agent, I'd copy all of it.
Let's wrap it into a reusable Agent class instead.
Step one: the Agent class. Same Maven project as before, with the Anthropic Java SDK, version three.
lines.tts: Step one: the Agent class. Same Maven project as before, with the Anthropic Java S D K, version three.

lines.say: I create Agent dot java.
An agent is four things: a name, a system prompt, a list of tools, and a function that runs those tools.
The system prompt is the agent's role. This is what makes a reviewer different from a writer.
And each agent gets only the tools it needs.
The client is shared. Every agent talks to the same API, with your key from the environment.
lines.tts: The client is shared. Every agent talks to the same A P I, with your key from the environment.

lines.say: Step two: the agent loop. It's the loop from episode one, wrapped in one method: run.
Every run starts a fresh conversation. The agent sees only its own system prompt and its own task. That's its own context.
When Claude stops asking for tools, run returns the agent's answer as text. So another agent can use it.
The rest is the same as before: run every tool the agent asked for, and send all the results back.
One change: the loop stops after ten turns, so an agent can never run forever.
And in SDK version three, the method that sends tool results is called add user message of content block params.
lines.tts: And in S D K version three, the method that sends tool results is called: add user message of content block params.

lines.say: Step three: give the Reviewer a tool. Here's the code it will review: a small user service, with bugs on purpose.
Can you spot them? We'll see if the Reviewer does.
Now FileTools dot java. The tool is called read file, and it takes a file name.

do.text:
// The Reviewer's only tool: read a file from the sample folder
public class FileTools {

    static final Tool READ_FILE = Tool.builder()
            .name("read_file")
            .description("Reads a Java file from the sample folder. "
                    + "Use it to see the code before reviewing it.")
            .inputSchema(Tool.InputSchema.builder()
                .properties(Tool.InputSchema.Properties.builder()
                    .putAdditionalProperty("name", JsonValue.from(
                        Map.of("type", "string")))
                    .build())
                .required(List.of("name"))
                .build())
            .build();

lines.tts: Now FileTools dot java. The tool is called read file, and it takes a file name.

lines.say: The real work is a plain Java method. It only reads files inside the sample folder, and returns errors as text.
That check matters: an agent should never read files you didn't plan for.
Step four: build the team, in ReviewTeam dot java.
lines.tts: Step four: build the team, in ReviewTeam dot java.

lines.say: Two agents, created from the same class.
The Reviewer is a strict senior reviewer. It gets the read file tool, and lists real bugs only.
The Writer has a different role, and no tools at all.
Here's how they work together: the Reviewer's notes become the Writer's task. The Writer never sees the code. Only the notes.

do.match: String report = writer.run("Write the report:\n" + notes);
do.label: Notes → Writer

lines.say: That's a multi-agent system: two agents, each with one job.
Let's test it. First, an offline check of the tool. No API key needed.

Now the real team.

lines.say: The Reviewer used its tool to read the file. Then the Writer took over.
It found all three bugs, and the Writer explained them in plain words. Each agent did one job.

cards.title: Only the tools it needs
cards.text: The Writer doesn't need to read files

cards.title: Pass results, not history
cards.text: Short notes keep each context clean

cards.title: Cap every loop
cards.text: A max number of turns per agent

lines.say: Four tips for your agent team.
One: give each agent one job, with a short, clear system prompt.
Two: give each agent only the tools it needs. Our Writer doesn't need to read files.
Three: pass short results between agents, not the whole conversation. That keeps every context clean.
And four: cap every loop. More agents means more ways to run forever.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: A multi-agent system = **agents with one job each**
Each has its **own prompt, tools and context**
Costs more tokens: [[start with one agent]], split when it struggles

lines.say: Let's recap.
A multi-agent system is several agents, each with one job.
Each agent has its own system prompt, its own tools, and its own context.
It costs more tokens. So start with one agent, and split only when it struggles.
